Onboarding — round 5

Two corrections on round 4, plus one reversal. The device keyboard is native, not drawn — C3 no longer renders a custom keypad. Round 4's "not glassmorphism" claim didn't survive contact with its own CSS — gradient fills and inset white highlights on nearly every surface, stripped and replaced with HeroUI's actual defaults: flat semantic fills, generous radii, one nearly-invisible shadow token. The one exception, at your call: “Finally clear.” keeps its gradient — round 5 had flattened it, you compared both and chose the colour back, so it returns with a third stop that holds gold through “Finally” and lands the teal on “clear.” Everything else that glowed is now a flat fill or a border. Three expressive surfaces in 31 frames: the N2 selected account-type tile, the N4 hero — both pre-existing shipped component code you chose — and that headline. Nothing moves — the four-track shell, the permanent message rail, the reserved credit slot and the fixed N4 slots are unchanged from round 3.

MA-onboarding-redesign · pre-gate-1 · 390 pt frames · zero emoji — every glyph is inline SVG standing in for a MaterialCommunityIcons name, legend at the bottom · fonts substituted (Sora → Avenir Next, Inter → Helvetica Neue) because the published artifact blocks external hosts · all motion fires once, nothing loops, nothing at all under reduce-motion. Rationale and costs at the bottom.

A · The shell structure frozen

Unchanged from round 3 and not up for renegotiation: header 56, progress rail 55, a flexible content viewport, and a footer of 34 pt status track + 52 pt CTA. The status track is always mounted and never empty — idle it carries the one footnote that screen genuinely wants, on failure the error replaces that footnote in the identical box. Round 4 dressed this shell in glass — gradient fills and inset white highlights on the header, the footer and the CTA. Round 5 strips all of it: the header and footer are a flat background with a hairline rule, the progress segments are a flat --accent fill, and the CTA is HeroUI's own primary button — flat --color-accent, border-width: 0, no gradient, no ring, no shimmer. See the rationale for exactly what "glass" meant here and what replaced it.

A3 · Status track, failed error
Couldn't save that. Your account is safe — tap Review setup to try again.
Review setup
Retry is the CTA itself, so no second button ever appears and the footer never grows. Two lines of danger-coloured copy is the widest case the track must hold — measured against the longest error string.
Contrast: --danger #E05A42 on --background = 4.81:1 — passes AA for body text. The track is announced as a live region so a screen reader hears the failure without moving focus.

Failure. Same box, same height, same CTA position. Tapping the CTA retries the failed step — it never re-inserts an account.

B · N1 — Welcome hero: Broadsheet headline · currency · CTA: Aurora

A three-way mix, and the seam is deliberate. Broadsheet owns the composition: a giant 01 ghost numeral at 5% opacity tied to step 1 of 4, a 34 pt gold rule, and a 42 px left-aligned headline — no card stack, no illustration, no centred block. Aurora's light survives in exactly one place: the gradient-filled Finally clear. Round 5 replaced it with flat gold; the user compared both and chose the gradient back, so it returns — now with a third stop at 45% that holds the gold through “Finally” and lets the turn to teal land on “clear.”, rather than washing teal across the whole line. The radial-gradient halo that used to sit under the selected currency row does not come back: selection is HeroUI's own language — accent border, --accent-soft fill, the Radio circle turning solid accent. Light marks the brand moment; colour marks state. The two-hue ambient wash behind the screen (gold top-left, Nile teal right) also stays — a base-canvas colour, not a material sitting on a surface. Round 3 keeps the semantics: this is still a RadioGroup of two 76 pt rows that each state the consequence of the choice, not a tablist.

B5 · Empty n/a — by rule
N1 has no empty state.
Business rule 5 pre-selects EGP, so the screen is fully populated on first paint and there is nothing to load. App startup owns migrations, the onboarding store and the account snapshot before any onboarding route mounts, so N1 never renders a skeleton either.
Drawing an invented blank frame here would misrepresent the flow. The only states this screen has beyond the default are B2, B3 and B4.
If startup itself fails, the existing app-level startup error screen owns it — outside this scope.

Stated, not drawn — deliberately. The four-state floor exists to catch forgotten states, not to license invented ones.

“Finally clear.” — the user's call, and the one spike this design still carries. Round 5 shipped flat gold and closed this out. The user compared it against round 4's gradient and chose the gradient: it “gives feeling”. That is a legitimate call on a brand moment, it is the only screen where the app gets to be expressive rather than functional, and it is now the design. What it costs is honesty about the risk, not the decision.

Gradient-filled text means react-native-svg's Text with a LinearGradient fill, and nothing in this codebase does that today. @tariq spikes it on a real mid-range Android device at step 2, checking three things specifically: that it scales with dynamic type rather than rasterising at a fixed size; that the accessibility label survives (the frames carry role="heading" aria-level="1" + aria-label="Finally clear." because SVG text is not read as text); and that it does not regress first-paint on the app's very first screen.

The fallback is flat --accent gold and costs nothing — same size, same position, same line break, zero layout change. If the spike is anything but clean, ship the fallback; nothing structural depends on this. Contrast passes either way: the three stops measure 9.55, 7.78 and 6.15 against --background, all clear of AA, and the flat fallback is 7.78.

C · N2 — Add your first account tiles: Vault form: Broadsheet shared form

This is where first-run onboarding is actually abandoned, so this is where the design spends — and it is a two-way mix. Vault owns the type tiles: the selected one gets HeroShell's full formula — diagonal gradient, 26 px grid texture, corner glow, hairline gold border, a gold icon chip — and the other four stay flat surface. That is the whole point: Bank reads as chosen at a glance rather than merely outlined. Broadsheet owns the form: sentence-case labels tight to the field, balance and currency sharing one row because currency is short, and a tighter, less uniform stack than five identical full-width boxes.

Frozen from round 3 and untouched: the 3-column, 5-tile, left-aligned grid at 114 × 76 pt; the permanent 20 pt message rail under every field, carrying helper copy when the field is clean and the error when it isn't; and the reserved credit-card slot — a dashed one-line hint when the type isn't Credit Card, the real fields in the same place when it is.

APR appears inside the card block, below the switch — the block grows downward and the header, rail and CTA are untouched. Two failures at once: a field-level error in its own rail, and a save-level error in the status track. They never fight for the same space.

What the Vault tile costs, and the cheaper version. The selected tile is four stacked layers — a LinearGradient, an SVG grid Pattern, an absolutely-positioned glow View, and the content — where round 3 had one flat fill. That is three extra render nodes on exactly one tile, mounted once and re-rendered only on selection change; it is the same node count hero_shell.tsx already ships on the dashboard, so there is no new risk, just a small one. The cheaper version: drop the grid Pattern and keep gradient + glow. It removes the SVG node entirely and, at 114 × 76 pt, the 26 px grid is barely legible anyway — I'd take that trade if @tariq wants it. Do not drop the gradient; that is the whole reason the choice reads at a glance.
What I deliberately dropped: the July field list had both “Amount currently owed” and a separate “revolving balance”. Two “how much do you owe” boxes on someone's first-ever screen is a comprehension trap. Balance relabels to Amount currently owed and that is the only owed field. If the revolving_balance column must be non-null at creation, [layla] decides what it derives from — it should not become a fifth question.

D · The 32-colour sheet selection: Aurora

Structure frozen from round 3: all 32 visible at once, no scrolling, an 8-column chart where column position means the same family in both tone blocks — Nile Teal rich sits directly above Nile Teal soft. Round 4 gave the selected swatch a hue-matched radial-gradient glow and every tile a glossy top-highlight/bottom-shade bevel — both gone. Selection is now the same flat, bordered indicator HeroUI itself uses: a 2 pt --foreground ring plus a check glyph, contrast-picked per swatch. Every tile is a flat colour rectangle; the colour is the content, nothing needs to make it glow to prove it was chosen.

The tick is near-black on Sand soft and bone-white on Nile rich in D1 — picked per swatch from a contrast table, never assumed white. The border ring is drawn in the cell's permanent 3 pt padding, so selecting never resizes a tile or reflows the grid.

Geometry and targets. 8 columns at 390 pt with 16 pt sheet padding and a 4 pt gap gives a cell of 41.25 × 44. That is 2.75 pt short of the 44 pt floor horizontally, so each cell carries hitSlop={{left: 2, right: 2}} → 45.25 × 44 effective, with no overlap because the gap is 4. Colour is never the only signal: the preview row names the family and tone, and each tile announces “Nile Teal, rich, selected”. Sheet uses the project Sheet at size="md" with a sticky footer; the grid does not scroll, so there is no gorhom scrollable inside it at all.
The RadialGradient underlay is gone; nothing replaced it. Round 4 gave four things a glow — the currency row, the account colour dot, the selected swatch, the type tile — each an absolutely-positioned sibling View filled with a react-native-svg RadialGradient. Three of those four are now a flat color-mix() background or border colour: zero extra nodes, zero new implementation risk, nothing for @tariq to spike. The fourth, the type tile's corner glow, survives — but it is not new: it is hero_shell.tsx's own RadialGradient, already shipped and rendering on the dashboard today. So the only remaining gradient underlay on this entire page is code that already exists.

E · N3 — Add more accounts composition: Broadsheet derived — no round 2 frame

Round 2 never drew this screen, so this is derived rather than adapted — and I derived it from the two directions the neighbouring screens use, not a third one. Broadsheet gives it the composition: a 03 ghost numeral, the gold rule, a left-aligned heading, no centred celebration block. The account list is a flat ListGroup: round 4 gave it a gradient fill and an inset top highlight to read as a "layered surface" — that's gone, it's now the same flat --surface fill plus a hairline border every list on this page uses, and it still reads as the subject of the screen because it's the only dense content block on an otherwise spacious page, not because of applied material. The success chip is HeroUI's own soft-success variant — a flat --color-success-soft tint, no glow — and it stays a 28 pt chip, because round 3's call stands: the only question here is “is anything missing?”, and you answer that by looking at the list, not at a trophy.

Also unchanged from round 3: each row shows its balance in its own currency, and there is no running total — a total needs a rate, a rate might not exist, and deferring that to N4 keeps the conversion problem in exactly one place.

F · N4 — Ready to start hero_card.tsx, verbatim

The hero here is the dashboard's hero_card.tsx, verbatim: HeroShell's diagonal gradient, the 26 px grid Pattern at 3%, the 160 px gold corner glow at 0.18, the hairline border, the 24 pt gold circle chip on the label row, and the overlayWhite7 pill row underneath. Whatever premium feeling that card earns on day 30, this screen borrows on minute 1 — and it costs nothing to build, because the component already ships.

One deliberate deviation, and it is Marcus's call, reversible. hero_card.tsx:141 sets its number at ms(32) — essentially round 3's 31 px, the size round 2 correctly said “undersells the one number onboarding exists to produce”. I have taken it to Type.amountEntry (40 px), a scale that already exists in theme.ts. Two consequences, both handled: the value slot grows from 40 pt to 52 pt (40 px Sora at 1.25 line-height needs ~50; 52 is also Size.ctaHeight, so it is not a new number), and the whole card grows by about 20 pt — 12 of that the slot, the rest hero_card's pill row replacing round 3's single meta line. Composed from the tokens: 12+24+12+52+4+34+12+24+20 = 194, against round 3's 174. N4 has roughly 150 pt of slack at base text size, so it absorbs this without scrolling. F0 re-proves the slot at the new size.

The three rules from round 3 survive unchanged. One — the value slot never wraps: one line, vertically centred, with a step-down rung rather than a reflow. Two — the caption slot is never empty: reserving two lines for a caption that only appears in one state would be dead space in the other six, so every state has a caption that earns it. Three — the number is never coloured by sign: not red for negative, not green for positive. It is Colors.dark.gold in every state because that is what hero_card does — the sign carries the fact, the caption carries the meaning, and the first number MoneyApp shows a person who legitimately owns a credit card is not painted as a failure.

The re-proof, and the finding that made the deviation cheap. Outer dashes = the 52 pt value slot · inner dashes = the 34 pt caption slot. Both are annotation only; they do not ship. The usable line width is 390 − 32 (screen) − 24 (card) = 334 pt.

Round 3 wrote EGP 148,250.00 — currency before the number, at full size. hero_card puts the currency after, as a 16 px suffix at 0.8 opacity. That single arrangement change buys back roughly 90 pt of line — which is most of what the jump from 31 to 40 px costs. So −1,234,567.89 EGP, the string round 3 had to step down to 22 px, now renders at the full 40 px (case 2). The step-down rung is still there and still needed, it just triggers later: drop to 28 px when the formatted amount exceeds 13 characters (case 3 is 14). Exchange rate needed renders at 22 px with the warning glyph, well inside a box already proven to hold a 40 px line.

Contrast on the hero gradient, computed against its lightest stop #223060 — the worst case: gold #D4A44C = 5.56:1, warning #E8B130 = 6.50:1, foreground #F0EBE3 ≈ 14:1. All pass AA, and the number is large text anyway.

Reference frame, not a screen. This is the whole answer to “does a 40 px number still fit the slot that used to hold a 31 px one, in every state including the one that puts a 20-character sentence there”. Yes, at 52 pt.

Rationale

Round 5 — what "glassy" actually was, and what replaced it

Round 4's rationale claimed it wasn't using glassmorphism. Counting the actual CSS said otherwise: 22 inset 0 1px 0 rgba(255,255,255,…) top-highlights, 31 inset shadows total, 28 linear-gradients, 15 radial-gradients. Nearly every surface — input boxes, list groups, the sheet, the back button, switches, keyboard keys, colour tiles — got a gradient fill plus a faint white top-edge highlight. That pairing, gradient fill + inset highlight, is the specific recipe that reads as "glass" regardless of what the rationale called it, because it's simulating a translucent, lit-from-above surface on top of a flat one.

I read the primitives this app actually ships instead of continuing to describe my own invention. Ground truth, node_modules/heroui-native/src/styles/components/*.css:

surface.css — .surface__root { box-shadow: var(--shadow-surface); }, no border, no gradient. In this app's dark theme --shadow-surface resolves to 0 0 0 0 transparent (variables.css:146) — HeroUI surfaces carry literally no shadow in dark mode. button.css — .button__root--variant-primary { background-color: var(--color-accent); } on a root with border-width: 0. Flat fill, no ring, no sheen. radio.css — .radio__indicator is a flat --color-field circle that becomes flat --color-accent when --is-selected; no glow anywhere in the file. chip.css — every variant is a flat background-color, including the "soft" tints (--color-accent-soft etc., theme.css:79-97: color-mix(in oklab, X 15%, transparent) — a flat tint, not a gradient). bottom-sheet.css is the one exception: its content background carries box-shadow: var(--shadow-overlay), which in dark mode is 0 0 1px rgba(255,255,255,.2) inset — a genuinely subtle 1 px edge, nothing like round 4's layered highlights.

HeroUI's language, in one sentence: solid semantic fills, generous radii, one nearly-invisible shadow token, selection expressed as a colour and border change, never as light. Round 5 matches it. Every gradient fill and inset highlight is stripped from input boxes, the colour trigger row, list groups, the bottom sheet, the back button, the trust row, the card-details block, switches, colour swatch tiles and the CTA. The currency-row halo, the account-colour ambient ring, and the colour-swatch glow ring — all radial-gradient underlays marking a selection — are replaced with HeroUI's own selected-state language: an accent border plus an --accent-soft fill, the same formula .radio__indicator--is-selected uses.

What survives, and why it isn't the same defect. Two gradient surfaces remain: the selected N2 account-type tile and the N4 hero. Both are hero_shell.tsx's own formula — a real, already-shipped component the user explicitly chose in round 3, not a glass effect invented for this scope. And the N1 ambient wash (two low-opacity radial gradients behind the whole screen) also stays: it's the screen's base canvas colour, not a material sitting on top of a surface — no blur, no translucency, no white edge highlight, nothing pretending to be lit glass. Two gradient surfaces plus one atmospheric background, in a flow of 31 frames, is not the glassy theme.

The shimmer — cut, not kept. Round 4's CTA shimmer worked as one ingredient in a five-part "premium jewel button": gradient fill, inset sheen, a soft gold ring, and a one-shot light sweep, all reinforcing the same "this is special" read. Take away the gradient, the sheen and the ring — which this correction requires — and the sweep loses the context that made it read as a considered effect rather than a stray flash across an otherwise perfectly flat, unadorned button. On HeroUI's actual primary Button, a diagonal light streak with nothing else around it looks tacked on, not arrived. So it's cut everywhere, not just toned down: the CTA is flat --color-accent, full stop, and the "app feels alive" job on first paint is carried by the four staggered rise-ins instead, which are HeroUI-neutral (plain opacity/translateY, not a material effect).

The gradient headline — reversed by the user, and correctly. Round 5 stripped it to flat gold on the reasoning that "normal" should also retire an unverified spike. The user reviewed both side by side and chose the gradient back: it "gives feeling". They are right about the thing that matters — N1 is the one screen in this flow whose job is to make someone feel like the app is worth setting up, and flat gold on a flat background does not do that. The mistake in round 5 was bundling a brand decision into a material correction: stripping glass off ordinary surfaces was right, and it should not have taken the one expressive element with it.

So the gradient returns, with one refinement rather than a straight revert: a third stop at 45% holds gold through "Finally" so the turn to teal lands on "clear." The engineering risk is unchanged and is not resolved — see the risk note in section B. It is a step-2 spike for @tariq with a zero-cost fallback, which is a normal thing for a design to carry, not a defect.

Why a per-section mix reads as one design and not three

Because the three directions were never three styles — they were three answers to “what carries emphasis?” Broadsheet says scale. Vault says material. Aurora says light. A design that used all three on the same element would be noise. This one gives each a different job, and the jobs do not overlap:

Scale is how a screen introduces itself. N1 and N3 both open with the same three-part Broadsheet move — ghost numeral, 34 pt gold rule, oversized left-aligned headline. N4 uses the rule and the eyebrow without the ghost, because by then the number is the biggest thing on screen and a second giant numeral would compete with it. N2 skips the composition entirely: it is a form, and a form's job is not to introduce itself.

Material is how the app says “this is the object”. There are exactly two gradient surfaces in the whole flow — the selected account-type tile and the N4 hero — and they are the same gradient, HeroShell's, because they are the same statement: this is the thing you chose, and this is the thing you made. Round 2 warned that HeroShell dilutes if you apply it to six things on one screen. There is never more than one per screen here.

Light was how round 4 acknowledged you; colour does that job now. Every glow round 4 drew marked a current selection — the chosen currency row, the chosen colour dot, the chosen swatch. That was the right instinct pointed at the wrong tool: HeroUI already has a way to mark a selection, and it isn't light, it's an accent border plus an accent-soft fill (exactly what .radio__indicator--is-selected does). Round 5 keeps the instinct — selection is still the only thing that visibly changes state on these screens — and drops the glow that carried it. The currency row in B2 still visibly moves when you tap the other option; it's a colour and border change now, not a halo.

The seam that could have shown is N1, where Broadsheet and the ambient wash meet. It holds because they stack rather than compete: Broadsheet owns the layout, the ambient wash sits behind all of it as a static base colour, and there is no card, no gradient panel, no material hero on this screen — not even the CTA, which is flat like every CTA in the flow. N1 has zero gradient surfaces. The only two on the whole page are the N2 selected tile and the N4 hero, three and four steps later.

What the richer treatments cost — implementation and mid-range Android

TreatmentBuilt fromCost
Vault selected tileLinearGradient + SVG grid Pattern + glow View3 extra nodes, one tile only, re-rendered on selection. Same stack hero_shell.tsx ships today. Cheaper: drop the grid Pattern.
N4 heroHeroShell + hero_card internalsZero — the component exists and is already on the dashboard. Only the font size and slot heights differ.
Ambient wash (N1)2 × RadialGradient in one full-screen SvgOne SVG, one screen, static. Cheapest thing on this page. No blur — expo-blur is not used anywhere.
Everything else round 4 glowedflat background-color / color-mix() tint, or nothingZero. Currency-row, colour-dot and swatch halos were each a View + RadialGradient underlay; all three are gone, replaced by a colour/border change that was already being computed for the selected state.
Broadsheet ghost numeralText at 5% opacity, absolutely positionedZero — one text node. No image, no vector art.
Headline "Finally clear."SvgText + 3-stop LinearGradientUnverified — the one open spike. One SVG text node on one screen, static, no animation. @tariq spikes it at step 2; flat --accent gold is the zero-cost fallback with identical geometry. See section B.
CTAHeroUI primary Button: flat fill, border-width: 0Zero. No shimmer, no ring, no sheen — see the shimmer note above.
Surfaces (fields, list groups, sheet, switches, tiles)flat background-color, hairline borderZero new nodes. elevation/shadow* unused except the sheet's single --shadow-overlay token.

The honest summary for a mid-range Android device: this is now a cheaper page than round 4, not just a flatter one. Round 2's Aurora column had a 2.6 s shimmer loop and a 4.2 s breathing orb and a 5 s pulsing hero glow; round 4 cut those three but added four static gradient-underlay pairs and a CTA shimmer; round 5 cuts those too. What's left that I'd actually watch on a real device: the N2 tile gradient re-rendering on every type tap (five taps maximum, tile is 114 × 76 pt), and the N1 full-screen SVG wash compositing under a scroll — which is why the wash is on the shell, behind the scroll view, not inside it. Everything else on the page is a flat colour.

Motion inventory — every animation on this page, and when it stops

AnimationWhereFires
Staggered fade + 10 pt rise, 500 ms, 0/120/240/360 msN1 four blocks, N3 two blocks, N4 three blocksOnce, on mount
Spring pop 0.32 sVault tile, on account-type selectionPer selection — a response to a tap, not a loop
Spinner rotationBusy CTA onlyWhile the write is in flight. It is a progress indicator, not decoration

Nothing loops. No breathing orb, no pulsing hero glow, no shimmer at all now — round 2 flagged looping motion as battery paid by everyone for delight almost nobody stays to see, and round 5 goes one step further and removes the one-shot CTA shimmer too, because it stopped reading as a considered effect once the button under it went flat (see the rationale note above). What's left — three staggered rise-ins per screen and one tap-triggered spring pop — is the entire motion budget for a four-screen flow a person sees exactly once. Under prefers-reduced-motion / AccessibilityInfo.isReduceMotionEnabled, neither runs at all.

Icon legend — no emoji, every glyph named

Round 3 used 49 emoji as iconography. That is gone: every glyph on this page is an inline SVG standing in for a MaterialCommunityIcons name the app already ships. @dev renders the real font glyph — do not ship these SVG paths, they exist only so this page can be self-contained with zero external hosts. Account-type names are taken verbatim from TYPE_OPTIONS in src/modules/accounts/components/account_type_pill.tsx.

Two notes carried from round 3 and unchanged. The status track is plain Typography, not Alert: Alert is a bordered box with its own padding, so putting it in the footer would make the footer taller in the error state — the exact defect the track exists to prevent. And the existing ColorSwatchPicker becomes the sheet's grid or is deleted; the three divergent swatch-row implementations named in scope.md collapse to one.

Where I reached outside the token set

Six places, all named rather than quietly absorbed. Items 1, 2 and 5 are unchanged from round 3; items 3 and 4 moved; item 6 is new this round.

1 · The token script doesn't emit everything. Colors.shared (hero gradient stops, cairoGold, overlayWhite7) and AcctTokens (the account palette) are real tokens in theme.ts / theme_tokens.ts but design:tokens omits both. I re-declared them in a clearly-labelled second :root block with each source file named. Worth teaching the script to emit them — round 4 needs them more than round 3 did, because the material treatments are built from exactly these values.
2 · Four of the sixteen colour families don't exist yet. AcctTokens ships 12. Jade, Indigo, Coral and Graphite come from the July functional doc and need adding — no migration, colours are stored as plain hex values.
3 · There is no input-height token. HeroUI's Input derives its height from padding and font size, so “44” is not written down anywhere. I drew fields at Size.dialogButton (44), which happens to equal TouchSize.min. An alias Size.fieldHeight = ms(44) would say what it means.
4 · The geometry constants the zero-shift contract is built on are still not tokens — and one changed value. The field message rail (20), the N4 value slot (52, up from 40 because of the number size), the N4 caption slot (34), and the footer status track (34). These are the load-bearing numbers in the entire design and they should be Size.fieldMessageTrack, Size.summaryValueSlot, Size.summaryCaptionSlot and Size.statusTrack so a unit test can assert them rather than device QA having to eyeball them. This is still my one real ask. Four constants — and the value-slot one is now doing more work than it was, because it is what stops the 40 px number from reflowing the card.
5 · Fonts. The published artifact blocks external hosts, so this page renders Avenir Next for Sora and Helvetica Neue for Inter. Sora is wider and squarer at display sizes, which matters more at 42 px and 40 px than it did at 28 and 31 — the N1 headline and the N4 hero number are the two things to look at hardest on real hardware. That is a gate-3 check, not a gate-1 one, but it is the specific thing to look for. Composed sizes like the option-row and tile min-heights are token arithmetic (Size.dialogButton + Spacing.xxl), which is legal, not a new value.
6 · The HeroUI "soft" tint isn't in this app's generated CSS either. This round's selection language leans on --color-accent-soft and --color-success-soft — real HeroUI Native theme tokens (heroui-native/src/styles/theme.css:79-97, color-mix(in oklab, X 15%, transparent)) that Uniwind resolves to native colour values at build time, not CSS custom properties this app exposes at runtime the way design:tokens's output does. I declared --accent-soft / --success-soft / --success-soft-fg in the supplementary token block, computed the same formula in srgb instead of oklab (consistent with how the rest of this page already approximates color-mix), and cited the source inline. In the real app this is just className="bg-accent-soft" or the HeroUI Chip variant="soft" prop — nothing to build, only something this mockup had to reconstruct to render at all.

Accessibility

Contrast, computed not assumed. Against --background #0F1923: --foreground ≈ 18:1 · --warning 9.09:1 · --accent 7.78:1 (this is now also the headline colour, previously a gradient) · --success 6.56:1 · --danger 4.81:1. All pass AA. Against the hero card's lightest gradient stop #223060: gold 5.56:1, warning 6.50:1. --muted is 2.36:1 — decorative only; it is the progress-rail track and never carries text. The two remaining gradient surfaces (N2 selected tile, N4 hero) sit behind their text, never under it directly, so neither changes these numbers.

Targets. Currency rows 358 × 76 · type tiles 114 × 76 · all fields and the colour trigger 44 tall · colour tiles 41.25 × 44 with hitSlop 2 horizontally → 45.25 × 44 · back button 36 visual with hitSlop 8 → 52 · secondary “Add another account” 52. The one to verify in review is HeroUI's BottomSheet.Close — it renders a size="sm" icon button and may need hitSlop to clear 44.

Dynamic type. Fixed tracks (header, rail, CTA) use explicit line-height and numberOfLines. Everything else grows into the scroll viewport: type-tile labels take a second line and the grid row grows in place; the N4 pill row wraps rather than truncating; the field message rail is a minimum height so long error copy at large sizes expands rather than clipping. The two things large text stresses hardest are the two Broadsheet headlines — 42 px on N1 and the 40 px hero number — and both have a documented answer: the headline reflows into the scroll viewport (N1 has ~130 pt of slack at base size), and the number takes the 28 px step-down rung. Progress announces “Step 2 of 4”; the segments themselves are hidden from assistive tech. Swatches announce “Nile Teal, rich, selected”. The status track is a live region. The gradient headline carries an explicit accessibilityLabel and accessibilityRole="image", because SVG text is not read as text by a screen reader — that label is not optional decoration, it is the only thing standing between a blind user and a silent first screen. It is also the first thing to verify in @tariq's spike, alongside whether the text scales with dynamic type rather than rasterising at a fixed size.

What I am deliberately not building

The separate revolving balance field (folded into “Amount currently owed”). An inline “add a rate” action on N4. A two-page credit form — the most robust answer to the geometry problem, rejected because it adds a mode to the shared form that Settings would inherit. Horizontally scrolling swatch rows. The N1 illustration and Vault's card-stack hero art — you chose Broadsheet's ghost numeral, and running both would put two competing focal points above the fold. Aurora's breathing orb and its looping shimmer — cut in round 3. Round 4's gradient-fill-plus-inset-highlight on ordinary surfaces — cut this round; see the rationale opener for what it was and why. Any glassmorphism or expo-blur proper — Android and web paint it as flat opaque colour, and this project doesn't install expo-blur at all. And no running total on N3, because a total needs a rate.

Open decisions — carried forward unchanged, not re-litigated

These are yours, they are stated in scope.md, and round 5 changes nothing about them — carried forward, not re-argued.

1 · What choosing USD actually promises. Designed for the cheap answer: the screen asks “Which currency do you think in?” and each option states a display consequence. Honest under the current architecture, where EGP is the storage currency. The expensive answer — base currency meaning the same thing in every module — is its own scope.
2 · --content-secondary is 4% under the AA floor, app-wide. 4.33:1 on background, 3.77:1 on surface. Handled inside onboarding by rule — anything you must read is full-strength, the muted colour is confined to genuinely redundant labels. Leave it and live with the rule, or lighten the token as separate work. Cross-scope either way. Note, updated: round 4's added depth (gradients, shadows) doesn't stand in for this fix anymore — round 5 is flat again, closer to round 3's surface language — so the rule is doing the same work it always was, undiluted by anything else on the page.
3 · The logo accent. Drawn with the teal dot nudged onto the card corner rather than over the stem of the folded M, so it stops reading as “Mi” at launcher size. Confirm or revert.

Two more that are mine to recommend and yours to overrule, both restated from round 3: 32 colours or 24 (16 families needs four new AcctTokens entries; 12 families fits the same grid with none — I prefer 32, because at 24 the picker stops reading as a complete chart), and the credit-card hint row (~60 pt permanently, on four types out of five, buying the thing this scope exists to fix).
